sittings.bodyEn: Scatterfocus is mind wandering you choose and can notice. You enter it by leaving attentional space free around a simple activity, such as a walk, a ride, or any motion that leaves room. The mode does three jobs together: it plans the future, it restores energy, and it connects ideas. A future intention needs a step back, because a task that fills the present leaves no room to choose what comes next. Use the mode when you want a solution, a new idea, or a rest, and keep hyperfocus for the block you still mean to finish. Most people avoid being alone with their thoughts, and one survey found that a large majority had spent no time at all relaxing or thinking the day before, which is why this practice has to be scheduled.

terms.hook: A chosen inward pass with spare attentional space, used to plan, rest, or connect.

sittings.bodyEn: In this mode, about twelve percent of thoughts concern the past, about twenty-eight percent the present, and about forty-eight percent the future. Past thoughts are easier to remember, which is why one sour message can feel like the whole hour. Reflection on a task needs the step back, because doing the task and examining your approach use attention in different ways. Future thoughts are mostly planning, often for later today or tomorrow, and researchers call that lean the prospective bias. You are about fourteen times more likely to think about the future while scattering attention than while locked on a task. Goals show up about four percent of the time when you are immersed, and about twenty-six percent of the time in this mode, so the gap between tasks should be a wander.

terms.hook: The lean, during a chosen wander, toward planning the near future.

sittings.bodyEn: Capture mode is a sit with a pen and paper, once or twice a week, for about fifteen minutes, with nothing else competing. Let the mind roam, and write what becomes actionable: people to contact, items you are waiting on, forgotten tasks, chores, and intentions you should set. Unresolved commitments sit near the front because the mind treats them as open, so this sitting makes them available to clear. The first minutes often feel dull, and that dullness is what turns attention inward until your thoughts are more interesting than the room. Stop when the timer ends, then repeat the sit a few days later, because another page usually fills even after a recent capture. Keep the notebook for this chosen wander, and leave it out of the hyperfocus block.

terms.hook: A timed sit where you write whatever actionable thought rises, with no other task.

sittings.bodyEn: Problem-crunching is for one large nonlinear problem, such as a job change, a hard relationship choice, a hire, or the shape of a big project. Review the problem on paper first, then hold it lightly while your thoughts turn it over. Stay with it for about thirty to sixty minutes, or for as long as you can remain interested, and stop when restlessness takes over. When you drift to something unrelated, or freeze on a single point, nudge attention back to the problem. The leaps are often ones a straight list would miss, because the mind is free to approach from the side. Use this tighter hold sparingly, because a habitual task will give you many of the same connections with less strain.

terms.hook: Hold one hard problem loosely, and guide attention back when it leaves.

sittings.bodyEn: Habitual scatterfocus is the style to practice most: do one simple thing you enjoy, and do nothing else, until the mind begins to move. A walk, laps in a pool, laundry, or a cup of coffee can be the anchor, and a simpler anchor connects more ideas than music or a book. Let the mind roam, including into the past, and guide it only when a loop is going nowhere useful. A better mood expands attentional space, brings more future thoughts, and makes the session easier to continue. The task is the rail that keeps you in the mode until the walk or the chore is finished. Keep a notepad nearby, because a connection you fail to catch disappears.

terms.hook: One simple, enjoyable task that leaves room for the mind to roam and connect.

sittings.bodyEn: The minutes between tasks are where this mode matters most, and a phone will fill those minutes if you carry it. Leave the phone behind for the walk to coffee, for lunch, and for the moment someone steps away from the table. While you do the anchor, check what is in attentional space, especially when the anchor is novel or pleasant, such as a simple game. Without that check, the game becomes the whole task and the wander never gets recorded. Any required simple chore already in the day can be the same practice. Write the useful bits before you pick the phone back up.

terms.hook: Look at what is in attentional space during a simple task, and write it before the phone returns.

sittings.bodyEn: A larger attentional space lets you hold more of an idea while you connect it, and hyperfocus is what grows that space. You combine dots you encoded while you were actually paying attention, so focused work stocks the later wander. Meta-awareness is the third support: people catch a wander only about five times an hour, while the mind is elsewhere nearly half the day. Wandering can occupy the regions that would have noticed it, which is why the check has to be deliberate. More frequent checks move thoughts toward the present problem and the future. The inward time also supports self-awareness, incubation, memory of meaningful experiences, empathy, and compassion. Practice both modes on purpose, because each one makes the other more useful.

terms.hook: Noticing what is in attentional space often enough to catch a wander and use it.

sittings.bodyEn: Boredom is the feeling of dropping into less stimulation, and a device in every gap removes that drop. A month of deliberately dull tasks produced the same travel through past, present, and future as habitual scatterfocus, with less desire to keep going. When stimulation falls, the mind hunts for any pacifier, including a mess to tidy or a screen to lift. Taking that pacifier skips the plan, the incubated idea, and the recharge that the gap was for. Chosen scatterfocus keeps the inward travel and gives it a purpose, so you get the useful part of the drop with a task you can stand. Treat the space between activities as part of the work, a pass that lets related thoughts settle near each other.

terms.hook: A drop in stimulation you allow on purpose, so the mind can plan and connect.

sittings.bodyEn: Block a capture sitting or a problem-crunching walk on the calendar, or name one simple daily act for habitual mode. Do it today, even for a few minutes. Most wandering in an ordinary day is accidental, and little of it is enjoyable. Watch how this private mode helps you, because it helps different people in different ways. Enter at least one of the three styles before the day ends, with a notepad in reach. Keep the style that produced a plan, a captured loop, or a connection you can use.

terms.hook: Capture writes what surfaces, problem-crunching stays with one problem, and habitual mode roams on a simple task.

sittings.bodyEn: Scatterfocus is a wander you enter on purpose, with spare attentional space for a plan, a rest, or a connection. Capture mode writes what surfaces, problem-crunching stays near one hard problem, and habitual mode lets a simple task carry the longest roam. Habitual mode is the one to practice most often. A phone in the gap replaces that roam with novelty. A check during the anchor keeps a pleasant task from swallowing the session. Focused work still matters, because it stores the dots and the space this mode later uses.
sittings.prompt: Which scatterfocus style should you practice most often?
choices: Capture mode, because open loops are the only useful thoughts
Problem-crunching, held tightly for every small choice
Habitual mode, one simple enjoyable task with attention to spare
Accidental drifting whenever a focus block gets hard
